title: Foreknowledge presupposes settled future truth
explanation: On the stipulated definitions, infallible prior knowledge that a future action will occur requires that the corresponding proposition be true prior to the act.
caveat: A temporalist may revise the account of ‘prior’; an atemporalist may replace foreknowledge with timeless knowledge.
objections: Reject the temporal formulation of divine knowledge.
Argue that knowledge can track a future truth without its being presently truth-valued.

title: Open and settled future
explanation: The two claims explicitly quantify over the same class of future free-action propositions and respectively deny and affirm universal present bivalence.
caveat: The conflict disappears if the claims concern different propositions, times, or senses of determinacy.

title: Timelessness and temporal succession
explanation: Under the definitions used here, one claim denies and the other affirms that God undergoes temporal succession.
caveat: Hybrid views may distinguish phases or senses of temporality; they should not affirm both claims without qualification.
objections: Adopt timelessness sans creation and temporality with creation.
Distinguish metaphysical time from another ordering relation.

title: Libertarian freedom and determination
explanation: Libertarian freedom was defined as incompatible with causal determination by prior conditions, while theological determination says every human action is so determined.
caveat: A compatibilist can retain freedom but not freedom in the stipulated libertarian sense.
objections: Restrict divine determination so that some actions remain undetermined.
Adopt a compatibilist analysis of freedom.

title: Theological fatalist argument
explanation: If God’s past belief is fixed and infallibly entails the later act, transfer of accidental necessity appears to make the act unavoidable; PAP then places pressure on libertarian freedom.
caveat: This is not encoded as a deduction. Ockhamists dispute that the relevant past belief is a hard fact; others reject transfer, PAP, or the temporal framing.
objections: Treat the past belief as a soft fact partly about the future.
Ground freedom in sourcehood rather than alternative possibilities.
Adopt timeless rather than prior divine knowledge.

title: Timeless knowledge described as prior
explanation: The definition of foreknowledge used here locates divine knowledge prior to events, while timelessness denies temporal location. A timeless knower may know future-to-us events, but not literally beforehand.
caveat: This is largely terminological if ‘foreknowledge’ is used loosely for knowledge of what creatures call the future.
objections: Replace FOREKNOWLEDGE with an atemporal knowledge claim.
Use ‘future’ relationally to creaturely time without temporally locating God.

title: Succession and intrinsic changelessness
explanation: Temporally ordered divine states appear to involve intrinsic change, while strong immutability denies it.
caveat: Mere temporal endurance need not entail intrinsic change; the pressure concerns the stronger claim that God has successively different intrinsic states.
objections: Hold that only God’s extrinsic relations change.
Distinguish temporal location from qualitative change.

title: Creative freedom’s alternatives
explanation: If God’s actual creative choice is free and such freedom requires an alternative, then a relevant alternative to this total creative choice must be possible.
caveat: This conclusion uses the broad alternative encoded in CONTINGENT-CREATION; finer-grained alternatives may require a more specific claim.
objections: Reject alternative possibilities as necessary for divine freedom.
Argue that only alternatives within creation, not non-creation of this total order, are required.

title: Simplicity and contingent effects
explanation: Critics argue that if God’s willing is identical with God’s necessary, simple being, it is difficult to explain how that willing has a contingent total effect rather than a necessary one.
caveat: This is a modal-collapse objection, not a formal consequence of simplicity alone. Classical replies distinguish necessary divine willing from contingent relations or effects.
objections: Distinguish God’s intrinsic act from its contingent extrinsic terminus.
Deny that a necessary cause must have its effect necessarily.
Use an account of Cambridge properties or contingent relations.

title: Middle knowledge’s libertarian subject matter
explanation: The stipulated middle-knowledge claim explicitly concerns counterfactuals of libertarian creaturely freedom.
caveat: Broader uses of ‘middle knowledge’ may concern counterfactuals without libertarian freedom; this dataset uses the Molinist sense.
